new_statements.translation: p.91: 'There are other linguistic facts different from those we have studied so far. These include, among others, intonation, accents and tones. In this chapter we shall study only the tones. [...] Given that, in tone languages, the latter have a distinctive function on a par with phonemes [...]' p.94: 'Of the five tones recorded, two have a distinctive function: the high and low tones. They are the basic tones of the language.' p.108: 'We are dealing with two level tones: the high tone and the low tone.'

new_statements.rule_in_words: Bàlòŋ (Balong, A13) is described as a tone language with two lexical tonemes H and L (surface falling, rising and a non-phonemic mid); the author explicitly names accent among prosodic phenomena but sets it aside and gives no rule for word-stress placement. The parallel Bafaw description (Neba 2011: tonemes H, L, R, F) and Limnyuy 2000 (two underlying tones) are likewise tone-only and silent on stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Only tangential: p.167 states that in loanwords the source-language accent is mapped onto a high tone (« la correspondance de l'accent avec le ton haut »); p.72 says the syllable carries pitch, intensity and duration features, without further analysis of intensity.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone statements concern lexical (citation-form) tones of the phonological word; mid tone arises only in connected speech. No word- vs phrase-level stress domain is discussed. Neba 2011 §2.4.4 notes a phrase-final (prepausal) glottal stop in Bafaw as the only phrase-edge prosodic effect described.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog bafa1247 'Bafaw-Balong' (ISO bwt) unites two varieties treated separately in the literature: Balong / Bàlòŋ (Guthrie A13; Kouoh Mboundja 2004 and Limnyuy 2000 describe the 'Bàlòŋ proper' reference dialect, Mbanga/Muyuka area) and Bafaw / Nfaw / Lefɔ' (Guthrie A10, Kumba; Neba 2011 in Chia et al., Konhouet 1990). The quoted statement is from the Balong description; the Bafaw description (Neba 2011) independently gives four tonemes H, L, R, F and is likewise silent on stress.

new_statements.quote: As can be seen from the data above, the -CV- verb root exhibits three different tonal melodies, namely: the H tone, the L tone and the HL tone. Despite these surface tones, Bàlòŋ verbs essentially have two underlying tones, the H and the L tones as will be discussed below.

new_statements.relation_note: Same picture as the existing Kouoh Mboundja 2004 statement: Bàlòŋ is described purely as a two-tone (H/L) language with no word-stress statement. Catalog record has an empty rule; this work does not supply one. Dialect: Bàlòŋ proper (Nlóŋ), the reference dialect, not Bàyi (§1.1.3, pp.5-6).
new_statements.rule_in_words: The thesis is a Lexical-Phonology tonology of the verb complex and the noun: two underlying tones H and L, surface HL/LH contours from tone linking, dissimilation, H-tone anticipation/spreading. The words stress, accent, prominence, intensity do not occur anywhere in the full text (checked also for letter-spaced scanned variants); nothing is said about where word stress falls or whether it exists.
new_statements.identity_note: Limnyuy 2000 analyses the Bàlòŋ proper (Nlóŋ) dialect, which she calls the reference dialect, as opposed to the Bàyi dialect (§1.1.3, pp.5-6); Kouoh Mboundja 2004 is also Bàlòŋ proper, Neba 2011 is the Bafaw (Nfaw) variety. Monikang 1989 describes Mokpwe = Bakweri (Bantu A22), a different language from Balong; it is wrongly listed under bafa1247.
